findings.title: Kafka consumer commit is invoked from a background thread instead of Arroyo's main loop
findings.body: `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` spawns a background thread (`self.commit_thread`) that periodically calls `self.commit_function(committable)`, which invokes Arroyo's `Commit` callback. In Arroyo, `KafkaConsumer` (wrapping `confluent_kafka.Consumer`) is not thread-safe and expects `commit` to be called on the main `StreamProcessor` thread (typically inside `poll()` or `submit()`). Calling `commit` from a separate thread races with `consumer.poll()` / rebalance callbacks in `StreamProcessor` and can also commit offsets after partition revocation.

findings.title: `FixedQueuePool` is instantiated on the factory and destroyed on the first partition rebalance
findings.body: `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__` creates a single `self.queue_pool = FixedQueuePool(...)`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` / `terminate()` calls `self.queue_pool.shutdown()`. In Arroyo, `create_with_partitions` is called every time partitions are assigned, and `close()`/`terminate()` is called on the active strategy whenever partitions are revoked or rebalanced. After the first rebalance, `self.queue_pool` has all of its queues and worker threads permanently shut down (and `offset_tracker` retains stale offsets from the old assignment), so subsequent strategies created by `create_with_partitions` will raise `queue.ShutDown` on `submit()` and stop processing any messages.

findings.title: Unbounded work queues provide no backpressure and can exhaust memory
findings.body: `FixedQueuePool` creates each `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (unbounded), and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `MessageRejected` or blocks. Because `StreamProcessor` polls Kafka as fast as `submit()` returns, the consumer will read messages into memory at Kafka network speed regardless of how slowly `OrderedQueueWorker` threads process them (contrary to the docstring claim of "Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). Under load or a slow downstream dependency, this will buffer an unbounded number of messages in memory until the process OOMs, and during `close()`/`join()` the workers cannot drain before `join_timeout`.

findings.title: `FixedQueuePool.shutdown` sets `worker.shutdown = True` before draining queues, dropping queued items
findings.body: In `FixedQueuePool.shutdown()`, `worker.shutdown = True` is set on every worker before `q.shutdown(immediate=False)` is called. Because `OrderedQueueWorker.run()` loops on `while not self.shutdown:`, any worker that finishes its current item (or wakes up from `q.shutdown`) immediately exits the `while` loop without draining the remaining items in `work_queue`, and without calling `join()`'s final offset commit. Consequently, on graceful shutdown (`close()`/`join()`), all still-queued messages are abandoned and completed offsets after the last 1-second tick are never committed.

findings.title: `OffsetTracker.get_committable_offsets` gets permanently stuck if a partition has non-contiguous offsets
findings.body: `get_committable_offsets()` iterates `for offset in range(start, max_offset + 1):` and breaks as soon as an integer is not in `all_offsets`. In Kafka, offsets within a partition are not guaranteed to be strictly consecutive integers (for example, compacted topics, transactional markers/control batches, or filtered messages that were not submitted). Furthermore, when a consumer starts up or rebalances and receives its first message at offset `N`, `last_committed` is `-1` and `min_offset` is `N`, which works for the first batch; however, if any single offset number is missing between two messages (or if a partition is reassigned at a higher offset after `last_committed` was set), `offset in all_offsets` is `False`, the loop breaks immediately, `highest_committable` never advances, `all_offsets` grows without bound, and no further offsets are ever committed for that partition.
